title: Light and the electromagnetic spectrum

lede: Everything in Topic 5, split into two bands. The non-negotiables are the ray diagrams, the definitions, the order of the spectrum and the uses and dangers you must have at your fingertips. sections.title: Reflection

parts.title: The law and the diagram
parts.html:
Law of reflection: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. The normal is a line at 90° to the surface at the point where the ray strikes. The angle of incidence $i$ is between the incident ray and the normal; the angle of reflection $r$ is between the reflected ray and the normal.

In the exam the marks for a ray diagram or a method are for four things, one each (June 2024 Q6(a)(ii)): mark the position of the mirror and of the rays; draw the normal, perpendicular to the mirror at the point of reflection; label the angle of incidence and the angle of reflection from the normal; use a protractor. Writing "angle of refraction" on a reflection diagram loses that mark.

parts.title: Specular and diffuse reflection
parts.html:
Specular reflection is from a smooth surface (a mirror, still water): parallel rays stay parallel after reflecting, because every ray meets a surface at the same angle, so you see a clear image.

Diffuse reflection is from a rough surface (paper, a wall): the law of reflection still holds for every ray, but the surface is at a different angle at each point, so the normals point in different directions and parallel rays are scattered in all directions — no image, but the surface can be seen from anywhere.

The exam point: the law applies to all surfaces (June 2024 Q6(a)(i)). Rough surfaces do not break the law; their normals just vary.

parts.title: Explaining diffuse reflection
parts.question: Explain why you cannot see your reflection in a sheet of white paper, even though the paper reflects light. (2 marks)
steps: Surface: the paper's surface is rough (uneven on a small scale), so the normal is in a different direction at each point.
Rays: each ray still obeys the law of reflection, but parallel rays are reflected in different directions (scattered) — diffuse reflection — so no image forms.

questions.text: A ray hits a mirror at 30° to the mirror's surface. What is the angle of incidence?
questions.explain: Angles are measured from the normal, which is at 90° to the surface: 90° − 30° = 60°.

questions.text: State the law of reflection. (1)
questions.model: • The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection (both measured from the normal).

questions.text: Describe how a student could show that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection using a ray box, a plane mirror, paper and a protractor. (3)
questions.model:
3 marks — one mark per row.

PointForWhat you need to write
1Set upStand the mirror on the paper, mark its position, shine a ray at it and mark the incident and reflected rays with crosses / draw along them.
2NormalRemove the mirror, join the crosses, and draw the normal at 90° to the mirror line at the point of reflection (using the protractor).
3MeasureMeasure the angles of incidence and reflection from the normal with the protractor; repeat for several angles.
  • June 2024 Q6(a)(ii): any three of mark the positions / draw the normal perpendicular to the mirror / label the angles from the normal / use a protractor. "Angle of refraction" is not accepted.

questions.text: Which is the correct explanation of diffuse reflection?
options: The surface breaks the law of reflection
The surface is rough, so the normal points in different directions at different points and rays are scattered
The surface absorbs all the light
The rays reflect back along their own path
questions.explain: The law holds everywhere; it is the direction of the normal that varies on a rough surface.

questions.text: Explain why a calm lake gives a clear reflection of the hills but a rippled lake does not. (2)
questions.model:
• Calm water is a smooth surface: parallel rays reflect parallel (specular reflection), so an image forms.
  • Rippled water is rough: the normal differs from point to point so rays are scattered (diffuse reflection) and no clear image forms.

checklist: State the law of reflection and draw the ray diagram with the normal
Measure angles of incidence and reflection from the normal
Explain the difference between specular and diffuse reflection
sections.blurb: Light reflects off a mirror so that the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence. Both angles are measured from the normal — the line at right angles to the surface — never from the surface.

sections.title: Refraction
equations: \text{into glass: slows down, bends towards the normal}
\text{out of glass: speeds up, bends away}

parts.title: The ray diagram
parts.html:
Three things every diagram must have: the normal at each surface (dashed, at 90° to the surface), the angle of incidence and angle of refraction marked from the normal, and arrows on the rays.

A ray along the normal (angle of incidence 0°) goes straight through without bending — it still slows down, but there is no change of direction. That is the answer to the "why does this ray not bend?" question (June 2023 Q8(a)(i), June 2024 Q6(b)(i)).

parts.title: Why it bends: the speed changes
parts.html:
Refraction is caused by a change in speed. Light travels more slowly in glass (or water) than in air. When a wavefront meets the boundary at an angle, the part that enters the glass first slows down first, so the wavefront swings round — the ray bends towards the normal. Leaving the glass, the first part out speeds up first, and the ray bends away from the normal.

On entering glass from airSpeedWavelengthFrequency
lightdecreasesdecreasesstays the same

The frequency cannot change — it is set by the source. Since $v = f \lambda$ and $f$ is fixed, the wavelength changes in proportion to the speed.

Sound is the other way round: it travels faster in water than in air, so it bends away from the normal going in. The June 2023 scheme gave 3 marks for "refraction is caused by a change in speed; sound speeds up entering water; light slows down entering water".

parts.title: Explain the bend
parts.question: A ray of light enters a glass block at an angle. Explain why the ray changes direction. (2 marks)
steps: Cause: light travels more slowly in glass than in air — the speed changes at the boundary.

Effect: the side of the wavefront that enters first slows first, so the direction changes: the ray bends towards the normal. (Mentioning the wavelength getting shorter is extra; "the glass is denser" on its own is not an explanation.)

questions.text: A ray enters a glass block along the normal. What happens to it?
options: It bends away from the normal
It does not change direction (but it slows down)
questions.explain: With the angle of incidence 0° there is no bending; the speed still drops.

questions.text: A ray of light passes from air into water at an angle. State what happens to its speed, its wavelength and its frequency. (3)
questions.model:
• Speed decreases.
  • Wavelength decreases.
  • Frequency stays the same.

questions.text: Explain why light bends when it passes from air into glass at an angle. (2)
questions.model:
• The light slows down (changes speed) as it enters the glass.
  • So the direction changes — the ray bends towards the normal (the part of the wavefront that enters first slows first).

questions.text: A ray enters a rectangular glass block at an angle and leaves through the opposite face. The emergent ray is…
options: parallel to the incident ray but shifted sideways
at a larger angle than the incident ray
questions.explain: The two bends cancel (towards the normal in, away from it out), so the ray leaves parallel to the way it came in, displaced sideways.

questions.text: A ray of light enters a glass block with an angle of incidence of 40°. State whether the angle of refraction is bigger or smaller than 40°, and why. (2)
questions.model:
• Smaller — the ray bends towards the normal…
  • …because light slows down in the glass.

questions.text: Sound and light both travel from air into water. Explain why they refract in opposite directions. (3)
questions.model:
• Refraction is caused by a change in speed at the boundary.
  • Light slows down entering water, so it bends towards the normal.
  • Sound speeds up entering water, so it bends away from the normal.

checklist: Draw the ray diagram for a ray through a rectangular glass block, with normals and angles
State which way the ray bends entering and leaving glass, and why (speed change)
State what happens to speed, wavelength and frequency on refraction
sections.blurb: Light changes direction when it crosses a boundary between materials because its speed changes. Into glass or water it slows and bends towards the normal; out again it speeds up and bends away.

sections.title: Total internal reflection and the critical angle

parts.title: Three cases
parts.html:
Definition: the critical angle is the angle of incidence (in the denser material, e.g. glass) for which the angle of refraction is 90° — the refracted ray travels along the boundary. For glass it is about 42°.

Total internal reflection happens when both conditions are met: (1) the light is travelling from a denser material towards a less dense one (glass → air, water → air); (2) the angle of incidence is greater than the critical angle. Then no light leaves: all of it is reflected inside, obeying the law of reflection.

You do not need a formula for the critical angle at GCSE — the definition, the diagram and the three cases are what the questions test (June 2025 Q7(c), 3 marks: "what happens at the critical angle and beyond it").

parts.title: Describe what happens as the angle grows
parts.question: A ray of light inside a glass block hits the glass–air surface. Describe what happens to the ray as the angle of incidence is increased from 20° to 60°. The critical angle of the glass is 42°. (3 marks)
steps: Below 42°: the ray refracts out of the glass into the air, bending away from the normal; as the angle of incidence increases, the angle of refraction increases (and stays bigger than the angle of incidence) — the first of the June 2025 Q7(c) points. (A weak reflected ray also stays inside; the scheme ignores it, so do not spend a line on it.)
At 42° (the critical angle): the angle of refraction is 90° — the refracted ray travels along the surface.
Above 42°: no light leaves; the ray is totally internally reflected back into the glass, with angle of reflection = angle of incidence.

questions.text: State what is meant by the critical angle. (1)
questions.model: • The angle of incidence (in the denser medium) at which the angle of refraction is 90° (the refracted ray travels along the surface).

questions.text: State the two conditions needed for total internal reflection. (2)
questions.model:
• Light travelling from a more dense to a less dense material (e.g. glass to air).
  • The angle of incidence is greater than the critical angle.

questions.text: The critical angle for glass is 42°. A ray inside the glass meets the surface at an angle of incidence of 50°. What happens?
options: It refracts out, bending towards the normal
It refracts out, bending away from the normal
questions.explain: 50° is above the critical angle, so all the light reflects back into the glass.

questions.text: A ray inside water (critical angle 49°) meets the surface at 30°. What happens?
options: It refracts out into the air, bending away from the normal
questions.explain: 30° is below the critical angle, so the ray leaves the water (and a little is reflected).

questions.text: A ray inside a glass block reaches the surface at exactly the critical angle. Describe the refracted ray. (1)
questions.model: • It travels along the surface of the glass — the angle of refraction is 90°.

questions.text: Explain how light travels along an optical fibre without escaping, even when the fibre bends. (3)
questions.model:
3 marks — one mark per row.

PointForWhat you need to write
1BoundaryThe light travels inside the glass core and meets the glass–air (or glass–cladding) boundary — going from a denser to a less dense material.
2AngleIt meets the boundary at an angle of incidence greater than the critical angle…
3TIR…so it is totally internally reflected each time, zig-zagging along the fibre; gentle bends keep the angle above the critical angle.

checklist: State what the critical angle is (the definition, not a formula)
Describe what happens below, at and above the critical angle, with a diagram
State the two conditions for total internal reflection
sections.blurb: A ray trying to leave glass into air bends away from the normal. At the critical angle the refracted ray runs along the surface; beyond it the ray cannot get out and is totally internally reflected.

sections.title: Colour: absorption and filters
equations: \text{reflects its own colour, absorbs the rest}
\text{filter: transmits its own colour, absorbs the rest}

parts.title: Absorb, reflect, transmit
parts.html:
Opaque objects: a red jumper reflects red light and absorbs the other colours. A white object reflects all colours; a black object absorbs all colours. Each colour is a different wavelength (frequency) of light, and a surface absorbs some wavelengths more than others — differential absorption.

Filters: a red filter transmits red light and absorbs all the other colours. White light through a red filter comes out red; red light through a blue filter — nothing (black).

Coloured light: an object can only reflect colours that are shining on it. A red object in blue light looks black; a white object in blue light looks blue.

parts.title: A colour explanation
parts.question: A blue car is parked under a yellow sodium street lamp (which gives out only yellow light). Explain what colour the car appears. (2 marks)
steps: What the car does: the car's paint reflects blue light and absorbs other colours.
What light is available: the lamp gives out only yellow, which the paint absorbs; there is no blue to reflect, so the car appears black (very dark).

questions.text: Explain why a green leaf looks green in white light. (2)
questions.model:
• The leaf reflects green light…
  • …and absorbs all the other colours (wavelengths) in white light.

questions.text: White light passes through a green filter. What comes out?
options: Green light only — the filter absorbs the other colours
questions.explain: A filter transmits its own colour and absorbs the rest.

questions.text: A red shirt is viewed in green light. What colour does it appear?
questions.explain: Red fabric reflects only red; there is no red in green light, so it absorbs the green and reflects nothing.

questions.text: Explain why a white sheet of paper looks red when viewed through a red filter. (2)
questions.model:
• The filter transmits only red light and absorbs the other colours.
  • The white paper reflects all colours, including the red that reaches it (or: only red light from the paper gets through the filter to your eye).

questions.text: State what happens to the light that is not reflected by a coloured object. (1)
questions.model: • It is absorbed (transferred to the thermal store of the object).

checklist: Explain the colour of an opaque object in white light (reflects / absorbs)
Explain what a coloured filter does (transmits / absorbs)
Predict what colour an object appears in coloured light
sections.blurb: White light is all the colours together. An object's colour is the colour it reflects; everything else is absorbed. A filter's colour is the colour it transmits.

sections.title: Lenses: converging, diverging and power
equations: f \text{ in m, } P \text{ in dioptres (D)}

parts.title: Shape, focal length, power
parts.html:
A converging lens is fatter in the middle (convex). Rays parallel to its axis are refracted so they meet at the principal focus F. The focal length $f$ is the distance from the centre of the lens to F.

A diverging lens is thinner in the middle (concave). Parallel rays spread out as if they had come from a focus on the near side; its focal length is counted as negative.

$$P = \dfrac{1}{f}$$ with $f$ in metres and $P$ in dioptres (D). A lens of focal length 0.5 m has power 2 D; one of focal length 0.1 m has power 10 D.

Shape and power: the more curved (fatter, thicker in the middle, smaller radius of curvature) the lens, the more it refracts the light, the shorter the focal length and the higher the power. The June 2025 scheme's two marks were "a more powerful lens has a shorter focal length" and "a more powerful lens has a smaller radius of curvature" — thicker, fatter, more convex or more concave allowed for the second, and "stronger" allowed for "more powerful". When the question is about increasing magnification (June 2022 Q1(b)(ii)) name the change — higher power / shorter focal length / fatter / more curved — rather than "a stronger lens" on its own, which the report called too vague.

parts.title: Comparing two lenses
parts.question: Lens A has a focal length of 10 cm and lens B a focal length of 40 cm. Compare their power and their shape. (2 marks)
steps: Power: $P_A = \dfrac{1}{0.10} = 10$ D; $P_B = \dfrac{1}{0.40} = 2.5$ D. Lens A is four times as powerful.
Shape: lens A is more curved (fatter in the middle), so it refracts light more and brings it to a focus closer to the lens — the shorter focal length goes with the higher power.

questions.text: State what is meant by the focal length of a converging lens. (1)
questions.model: • The distance from the (centre of the) lens to the principal focus — the point where rays parallel to the axis are brought together.

questions.text: Which lens has the highest power?
questions.explain: $P = 1/f$: the shortest focal length (0.1 m, 10 D) is the most powerful.

questions.text: Describe how the power of a lens depends on its focal length and its shape. (2)
questions.model:
• The shorter the focal length, the higher the power ($P = 1/f$).
  • A lens with a smaller radius of curvature (more curved, fatter, thicker in the middle) has a shorter focal length and so a higher power.

questions.text: What does a diverging lens do to a beam of parallel rays?
options: Brings them to a focus on the far side
Spreads them out as if they came from a focus on the near side
questions.explain: Diverging lenses spread rays; the focus is virtual, on the same side as the incoming light.

questions.text: A converging lens has a focal length of 12.5 cm. Calculate its power.

checklist: Describe what converging and diverging lenses do to parallel rays, and define focal length
Relate the power of a lens to its focal length and its shape
Use $P = 1/f$ with f in metres and the unit D
sections.blurb: A converging (convex) lens brings parallel rays to a focus; a diverging (concave) lens spreads them out. The focal length is the distance from the lens to the focus, and the power is 1 ÷ focal length: a fatter, more curved lens has a shorter focal length and a higher power.

sections.title: Electromagnetic waves

parts.title: Three facts and an equation
parts.html:
• All EM waves are transverse: the oscillations are at right angles to the direction the wave travels.
  • All EM waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum, $3 \times 10^{8}$ m/s (and almost the same in air). They slow down in glass and water — which is why they refract.
  • All EM waves transfer energy from the source to the observer (the absorber). The Sun's infrared warms your skin; a microwave oven's microwaves heat the water in food; a radio wave makes a current flow in an aerial. No particles travel — the wave carries the energy.

$$v = f \times \lambda$$ For an EM wave the speed is already known, so the question is always for $f$ or $\lambda$: $f = \dfrac{v}{\lambda}$ or $\lambda = \dfrac{v}{f}$. Convert GHz ($\times 10^{9}$), MHz ($\times 10^{6}$) and nm ($\times 10^{-9}$) first — the 2022 report: not converting gigahertz to hertz was the common error.

Don't confuse EM waves with sound: sound is a longitudinal wave that needs a medium and travels at about 340 m/s in air. June 2025 Q3(c)(i) asked for "one other example of a transverse wave": an electromagnetic wave (or ripples, or a wave on a string) scores; sound is longitudinal and does not.

parts.title: Wavelength of a radio wave
parts.question: A radio station transmits at 98 MHz. Calculate the wavelength of its waves. (speed = 3 × 10⁸ m/s)
steps: Convert: $f = 98\ \text{MHz} = 98 \times 10^{6} = 9.8 \times 10^{7}$ Hz.
Equation: $v = f \times \lambda \;\Rightarrow\; \lambda = \dfrac{v}{f}$
Working: $\lambda = \dfrac{3 \times 10^{8}}{9.8 \times 10^{7}}$
Units: m

questions.text: State three properties that all electromagnetic waves have in common. (3)
questions.model:
• They are all transverse waves.
  • They all travel at the same speed in a vacuum (3 × 10⁸ m/s).
  • They all transfer energy from a source to an observer (absorber).

questions.text: Which of these is NOT an electromagnetic wave?
questions.explain: Ultrasound is a high-frequency sound wave — longitudinal, needs a medium, about 340 m/s in air.

questions.text: A microwave oven uses a frequency of 2.4 GHz. Calculate the wavelength of the microwaves. ($v = 3 \times 10^8$ m/s)
Orange light has a wavelength of 600 nm. Calculate its frequency. ($v = 3 \times 10^8$ m/s)
questions.hint: 600 nm = 6.0 × 10⁻⁷ m; type the answer as 5e14.

questions.text: Give an example that shows an electromagnetic wave transfers energy from a source to an observer. (2)
questions.model:
• Example with the wave named: e.g. infrared from the Sun (source)…
  • …is absorbed by your skin (observer), which warms up (energy transferred to its thermal store). Other examples: microwaves heating water in food; light making a solar cell produce a current; radio waves inducing a current in an aerial.

questions.text: Light passes from air into glass. Which statement is correct?
options: Its speed and frequency both decrease
Its speed decreases, its wavelength decreases, its frequency stays the same
questions.explain: Frequency is fixed by the source; $v = f\lambda$, so wavelength falls with speed.

checklist: State the three facts: transverse, same speed in a vacuum (3 × 10⁸ m/s), transfer energy from source to observer
Give an example of an EM wave transferring energy
Use $v = f \times \lambda$ with $c = 3 \times 10^8$ m/s and the right prefixes
sections.blurb: Radio waves, light and gamma rays are all the same kind of wave: transverse electromagnetic waves that all travel at the same speed in a vacuum and transfer energy from the source to whatever absorbs them.

sections.title: The electromagnetic spectrum
equations: \text{radio, micro, IR, visible, UV, X, gamma}

parts.title: The order and the trends
parts.html:
A mnemonic for increasing frequency: Raging Martians Invaded Venus Using X-ray Guns. Radio waves have the longest wavelength (metres to kilometres) and lowest frequency; gamma rays the shortest wavelength (smaller than an atom) and highest frequency.

The spectrum is continuous: there are no gaps, and the groups overlap at their boundaries — a wave at the edge of the microwave region could equally be called a short radio wave. The names are groupings by wavelength, nothing more.

Visible light is the narrow band our eyes can detect, from red (longest wavelength, about 700 nm, lowest frequency) through orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo to violet (shortest, about 400 nm). Everything else in the spectrum is invisible to us, which is why we need detectors (aerials, thermal cameras, film) for the rest.

parts.title: Placing a wave
parts.question: Infrared, X-rays and radio waves are three parts of the spectrum. Put them in order of increasing wavelength and say which has the highest frequency. (2 marks)
steps: Increasing wavelength is right-to-left on the spectrum: X-rays, infrared, radio waves.
Highest frequency = shortest wavelength = X-rays (frequency and wavelength run opposite ways, since $v = f\lambda$ with $v$ fixed).

questions.text: Which list is in order of increasing frequency?
options: gamma, X-rays, UV, visible, IR, microwaves, radio
radio, microwaves, IR, visible, UV, X-rays, gamma
radio, IR, microwaves, visible, X-rays, UV, gamma
visible, UV, IR, X-rays, gamma, radio, microwaves
questions.explain: Radio has the lowest frequency, gamma the highest.

questions.text: State which part of the electromagnetic spectrum has the longest wavelength, and which has the highest frequency. (2)
questions.model:
• Longest wavelength: radio waves.
  • Highest frequency: gamma rays.

questions.text: Which colour of visible light has the shortest wavelength?
questions.explain: Red is about 700 nm, violet about 400 nm.

questions.text: Explain what is meant by saying the electromagnetic spectrum is continuous. (1)
questions.model: • There are no gaps between the groups — every wavelength from radio to gamma exists, and the named groups overlap at their edges.

questions.text: Why can we not see infrared or ultraviolet?
options: Our eyes can only detect a limited range of frequencies (visible light)
questions.explain: The eye detects only roughly 400–700 nm; IR and UV lie just outside that range.

questions.text: Microwaves and infrared are next to each other on the spectrum. Which has the higher frequency?
questions.explain: Infrared is further towards the gamma end, so higher frequency and shorter wavelength.

checklist: Recall the seven groups in order of increasing frequency (and the reverse)
State that the spectrum is continuous and that the groups overlap at their edges
State the order of the colours of visible light and that our eyes detect only this narrow range
sections.blurb: One continuous family of waves, grouped by wavelength. Learn the order both ways, and which way frequency, wavelength, energy and danger run.

sections.title: Uses of each part of the spectrum
equations: \text{one use per region, in the spec's words}

parts.title: The list
parts.html:

June 2023 Q6(c) (4 marks) asked for two EM waves and, for each, a use or effect that showed energy being transferred: one mark for the wave, one for the result. Credited pairs included microwaves — cooking (water molecules gain energy); infrared — thermal imaging; ultraviolet — fluorescent lamps; X-rays — seeing inside the body; gamma — sterilising equipment; radio — communication (oscillations of electrons in wires). A harm counts as a result too: infrared — skin burns; microwaves — internal heating of body cells; ultraviolet — damage to surface cells. A second example about visible light (already in the stem) scored 1 mark only.

parts.title: A use with a reason
parts.question: Explain why infrared is used in TV remote controls rather than visible light or radio waves. (2 marks)
steps: Use: the remote sends a coded pulse of infrared to the TV's detector — short-range communication.

Reason: infrared is invisible (so it does not distract, unlike visible light) and is easily produced and detected over a short range with a cheap LED and sensor; radio would need an aerial and a licence and is not needed for a few metres.

questions.text: Which wave is used to detect forged bank notes?
questions.explain: Security markings fluoresce — glow visibly — under ultraviolet.

questions.text: State one use of gamma rays and one use of X-rays. (2)
questions.model:
• Gamma: sterilising food / medical equipment, or detecting and treating cancer.
  • X-rays: medical X-rays (seeing bones), airport security scanners, observing the internal structure of objects.

questions.text: Which use goes with microwaves?
questions.explain: Microwaves pass through the atmosphere to satellites and are absorbed by water in food.

questions.text: Name two electromagnetic waves and, for each, give a use or an effect that shows energy being transferred to something. (4)
questions.model:
4 marks — one mark per row.

PointForWhat you need to write
1Wave 1A named wave, e.g. microwaves…
2Result 1…cooking: absorbed by water molecules in the food, which gain energy (heat up).
3Wave 2A second named wave, e.g. infrared…
4Result 2…cooking / heating: absorbed by the surface of food or skin, which warms (or thermal imaging: detected after being emitted by warm objects).
  • Any correct pair scores: UV — fluorescent lamp / disinfecting water; X-rays — image of bones (absorbed by bone); gamma — sterilising (kills microbes); radio — communication (makes electrons oscillate in the aerial).

questions.text: Explain why X-rays are useful for finding a broken bone. (2)
questions.model:
• X-rays pass through soft tissue (skin, muscle) but are absorbed by bone.
  • So the bone leaves a shadow on the detector / film, showing its shape and any break.

questions.text: Optical fibres carry signals using which waves?
questions.explain: Infrared and visible light are totally internally reflected along the glass fibre.

checklist: Give at least one spec use for each of the seven regions
Match a use to its wave when given the use
Give the energy-transfer reason behind a use (absorbed by water, passes through skin, makes a current in an aerial…)
sections.blurb: The spec lists the uses it will ask about. A question usually wants the wave and a reason it suits the job, or the wave and the energy transfer that makes the use work.

sections.title: Dangers of electromagnetic radiation

parts.title: The four harms

sections.title: Every body radiates: intensity and wavelength

parts.title: Intensity and wavelength distribution
parts.html:
All bodies emit radiation. You, the desk, an ice cube — anything above absolute zero gives out electromagnetic waves, spread over a range of wavelengths. At room temperature almost all of it is infrared, which is what a thermal camera sees.

Two things change as an object gets hotter:

  • The intensity (power radiated per square metre) increases — at every wavelength, and so in total.
  • The peak wavelength — the wavelength at which most is emitted — gets shorter (the distribution shifts towards higher frequency).

So a poker in a fire first radiates only infrared (invisible), then as it heats the peak moves into the visible: dull red, then orange, yellow, and finally white when it emits across the whole visible range. The Sun's surface (about 5800 K) peaks in the visible; a cooler red star peaks at longer wavelengths.

parts.title: Describing the change
parts.question: A lamp filament is slowly heated from cold to white-hot. Describe how the radiation it emits changes. (3 marks)
steps: Cold: it already emits radiation — infrared only, invisible.
Intensity: as it heats, the intensity increases at every wavelength (it radiates more power).
Wavelength: the peak wavelength gets shorter — the emission moves into the visible, so the filament glows red, then yellow, then white.

questions.text: A cup of tea at 60 °C emits…
questions.explain: Every body radiates; at everyday temperatures the emission is almost all infrared.

questions.text: Describe two ways in which the radiation emitted by an object changes when its temperature increases. (2)
questions.model:
• The intensity (power radiated) increases.
  • The peak wavelength becomes shorter (shifts towards higher frequency / the visible).

questions.text: Explain why a piece of iron glows red when heated but white when heated much more. (2)
questions.model:
• As the temperature rises the peak wavelength gets shorter: at first only the red (longest-wavelength) end of the visible is emitted strongly.
  • Much hotter, it emits strongly across the whole visible range, and all the colours together look white.

questions.text: Two stars: one looks red, one looks blue-white. Which is hotter?
options: Colour does not depend on temperature
questions.explain: Shorter peak wavelength (blue) means higher temperature.

questions.text: A thermal-imaging camera can see a person in a dark room. Explain how. (2)
questions.model:
• The person's body emits infrared radiation because of its temperature (all bodies emit).
  • The camera detects the infrared; the person is warmer than the surroundings so emits more intensely and shows up brighter.

checklist: State that all bodies emit radiation, whatever their temperature
Describe how the intensity and the peak wavelength change with temperature
Explain why a heated metal glows red, then yellow, then white
sections.blurb: Everything with a temperature gives out electromagnetic radiation — mostly infrared for things around room temperature. The hotter the object, the more it radiates and the shorter the wavelength at which it radiates most.

sections.title: Key words: state what is meant by…

parts.title: The definitions
parts.html:
"State what is meant by" asks for the definition. Learn these as sentences.

TermWhat to write (mark-scheme form)Not this

sections.title: Ray diagrams that score, and the refraction practical
equations: \text{normal first, angles from it, arrows on rays}

parts.title: The rules for a ray diagram
parts.html:
1. Draw the normal first: a dashed line at 90° to the surface at the point where the ray hits (use a protractor or set square).
  2. Mark the angle of incidence between the incident ray and the normal, and the angle of refraction (or reflection) between the outgoing ray and the normal. Never measure from the surface.
  3. Put an arrow on every ray showing which way the light travels; rays are straight lines, drawn with a ruler.
  4. At a glass surface: towards the normal going in, away from the normal coming out; emergent ray parallel to the incident ray.

The June 2024 scheme for the reflection practical gave a mark for each of: marking the positions, drawing the normal perpendicular to the surface, labelling the angles from the normal, using a protractor. "Angle of refraction" written on a reflection diagram was rejected.

parts.title: The core practical: i against r in a glass block
parts.html:
Method (what a 4-mark "describe how" answer needs — June 2025 Q5(a) gave one mark each, any four, for: draw around the block; shine a ray at it; mark where the ray enters; mark where it exits; join the entry point to the exit point. "Draw the light rays" with no marking of points was worth 1 mark at most):

  1. Place the rectangular glass block on a sheet of paper and draw round it.
  2. Use a ray box (with a single-slit) to shine a narrow ray into one face at an angle.
  3. Mark the incident ray with two crosses (or a line) and the emergent ray where it leaves the block with two more.
  4. Remove the block, join the crosses to draw the rays, and join the entry and exit points to draw the refracted ray inside the block.
  5. Draw the normal at the entry point with a protractor (90° to the face); measure the angle of incidence and the angle of refraction from the normal.
  6. Repeat for several angles of incidence (e.g. 10° to 70°), and repeat each reading; plot angle of refraction against angle of incidence.

Draw a labelled diagram as part of the answer — the examiners say so every year.

Results: r increases as i increases, but not in proportion — the increase in r gets less for the same increase in i (a curve through the origin that gets less steep), and r is always smaller than i because the ray bends towards the normal. Those three statements were the three marks in Nov 2021 Q5(a)(iii). A ray along the normal ($i = 0$) does not bend. The emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray.

graph.alt: Angle of refraction plotted against angle of incidence for light entering a glass block: a curve through the origin that gets less steep; r is always smaller than i.

parts.title: Describing the method
parts.question: Describe how a student could use a ray box and a rectangular glass block to investigate how the angle of refraction depends on the angle of incidence. (4 marks)
steps: Set up: put the block on paper, draw round it; shine a single narrow ray from the ray box into one face at an angle.
Record the rays: mark the incident ray and the emergent ray with crosses; remove the block; join the crosses, and join entry point to exit point for the ray inside the glass.
Measure: draw the normal at the entry point with a protractor; measure the angle of incidence and the angle of refraction from the normal.
Vary and plot: repeat for at least five angles of incidence (repeat readings, average), and plot r against i.

questions.text: A student draws a ray diagram for light entering a glass block but measures the angles from the surface of the block. Explain what is wrong. (1)
questions.model: • Angles of incidence and refraction are measured from the normal (the line at 90° to the surface), not from the surface.

questions.text: Describe how to find the path of a ray of light inside a glass block, given that you cannot see the ray inside the glass. (2)

• Mark where the ray enters the block and where it leaves (crosses on the incident and emergent rays, and the block's outline).
  • Remove the block and join the entry point to the exit point with a ruler — the straight line is the refracted ray.

questions.text: A student plots angle of refraction against angle of incidence for light entering glass. Which describes the graph?
options: A straight line through the origin: r is proportional to i
A curve through the origin that gets less steep: r increases with i but not in proportion, and r is always less than i
A straight line with r greater than i
questions.explain: The ray bends towards the normal (r < i) and the relationship is not linear — the sine of the angles is.

questions.text: State two things the student should do to make the results of the refraction practical more accurate. (2)
questions.model:
• Use a narrow ray (single slit) and mark its position with crosses far apart, so the line through them is accurate; draw the normal carefully with a protractor / set square.
  • Repeat each angle and take a mean; work in a darkened room so the ray is clear.

questions.text: Which piece of equipment is needed to measure the angle of refraction?
questions.explain: Angles are measured with a protractor, from the normal.

questions.text: Describe how a student could show that the angle of incidence and the angle of refraction are not proportional. (2)
questions.model:
• Measure r for several values of i and plot a graph of r against i.
  • Proportional would give a straight line through the origin; the points lie on a curve (or $i \div r$ is not constant), so they are not proportional.

sections.title: Explaining refraction: speed, wavelength, frequency

parts.title: The wavefront picture
parts.html:
Think of the wave as a line of marching soldiers hitting a boundary at an angle: the soldiers that reach the slow ground first slow down first, so the line swings round towards the normal. The ray — at right angles to the wavefronts — changes direction. That is refraction: it is caused by the change of speed, and it only changes the direction if the wave meets the boundary at an angle.

Wave entering water from airSpeedDirection
lightslows downbends towards the normal
soundspeeds up (about 1500 m/s in water, 340 m/s in air)bends away from the normal

Frequency is fixed by the source — the waves arrive at the boundary at a certain rate and leave it at the same rate; none can pile up or vanish. Since $v = f\lambda$, if $v$ falls and $f$ is constant, $\lambda$ falls in the same proportion: light's wavelength in glass is about two-thirds of its wavelength in air.

What the examiners want written (June 2023 Q6(b), 3 marks): "refraction is caused by a change in speed"; the direction of the speed change for each wave; and nothing about transverse or longitudinal, which was ignored.

parts.title: A full explanation
parts.question: Explain why a ray of light bends towards the normal when it passes from air into glass, and state what happens to its wavelength and frequency. (4 marks)
steps: Speed: light travels more slowly in glass than in air.
Direction: the part of the wavefront that enters the glass first slows down first, so the wavefront turns and the ray bends towards the normal.
Frequency: the frequency is unchanged — it is set by the source.
Wavelength: because $v = f\lambda$ and $v$ falls with $f$ constant, the wavelength decreases.

questions.text: Explain why a wave does not change direction when it crosses a boundary along the normal, even though it changes speed. (2)
questions.model:
• The whole wavefront reaches the boundary at the same time, so every part slows down (or speeds up) together.
  • There is no difference in speed along the wavefront to turn it, so the direction is unchanged — only the speed and wavelength change.

questions.text: Light passes from glass into air. State what happens to its speed, wavelength, frequency and direction. (4)
questions.model:
4 marks — one mark per row.

3FrequencyUnchanged.
4DirectionBends away from the normal (if it meets the surface at an angle).

options: Glass has no effect on light
The frequency is set by the source: waves leave the boundary at the same rate they arrive
questions.explain: Waves cannot pile up at a boundary; the rate in equals the rate out.

questions.text: A stick in a pond looks bent at the water surface. Explain why, in terms of refraction. (2)
questions.model:
• Light from the submerged part of the stick speeds up as it leaves the water and bends away from the normal at the surface.
  • The eye assumes the light travelled in a straight line, so the underwater part appears higher / in a different position than it is — the stick looks bent at the surface.

questions.text: Water waves slow down as they move from deep water into shallow water. State what happens to their wavelength and their frequency. (2)
questions.model:
• Wavelength decreases (the waves bunch up).
  • Frequency stays the same.

sections.title: Finding the critical angle: method and graph
equations: \text{from a graph: read } i \text{ where } r = 90^{\circ}

parts.title: The method with a semicircular block
parts.html:
Use a semicircular glass block, because a ray aimed at the centre of the flat face enters through the curved face along a normal and so does not bend on the way in — all the refraction happens at the flat face.

  1. Put the block on paper, draw round it and mark the centre of the flat face.
  2. Shine a narrow ray through the curved face towards that centre; mark the ray and the refracted ray that leaves the flat face.
  3. Increase the angle of incidence in the glass (rotate the block or move the ray box) and watch the refracted ray bend further from the normal.
  4. Stop when the refracted ray just runs along the flat surface — the angle of refraction is 90° (equivalently: when total internal reflection just begins).
  5. Measure the angle of incidence from the normal with a protractor: that is the critical angle. Repeat and average.

These are exactly the June 2024 Q6(b)(ii) marks: increase the angle of incidence in the glass; until the refracted angle is 90° / the ray grazes the surface / TIR just begins; that angle of incidence is the critical angle; repeat and average. In June 2019 (Q4(b)) the same method was 4 marks, and an answer that sent the ray in through the straight edge was capped at 1 mark: say through the curved face, along a radius (towards the centre of the flat face).

parts.title: From a graph
parts.html:
A question may give angles of refraction (in air) for a ray leaving glass at several angles of incidence (in glass) and ask for the critical angle. The refracted angle is bigger than the incident angle and the curve steepens; it reaches $r = 90$° at the critical angle.

The method the June 2023 scheme gave three marks for: (1) extend (extrapolate) the curve smoothly, (2) until $r = 90$°, (3) read off the corresponding value of i — drop a line to the i-axis and label it. For the data below the curve reaches 90° at about 42°.

sections.title: Lens ray diagrams: real and virtual images

parts.title: The three rules and the four cases
parts.html:
1. A ray parallel to the axis refracts through the principal focus F on the far side (converging) — or away from the lens as if from F on the near side (diverging).
  2. A ray through the centre of the lens goes straight on undeviated.
  3. (Converging only) a ray through F on the near side leaves parallel to the axis.

Where the two rays from the top of the object cross, the top of the image is. If they only cross when traced backwards (dashed), the image is virtual.

Lens and object positionImageWhereUsed in

parts.title: Real or virtual — how to tell, and how to say it
parts.html:
A real image is where rays actually meet: it can be projected onto a screen and (for a single lens) it is inverted and on the opposite side of the lens from the object. A virtual image is where rays appear to come from: it cannot be projected, it is upright, and it is on the same side as the object.

June 2024 Q6(c) gave the mark for any one of: cannot be projected onto a screen; the rays do not actually pass through it; formed where imaginary (traced-back) rays meet; same side as the object; upright. "Not real" on its own scored nothing. June 2025 Q7(b) asked for an example of each and was "answered poorly": real — the image in a camera (a photograph), a projector image on a screen, the image on the retina, the image of a distant object formed by a converging lens; virtual — a magnifying glass, or the image seen through a diverging lens. The scheme said "do not accept telescope / microscope / glasses" and ignored "phone"; a plane mirror is not a lens.

Magnification $= \dfrac{\text{image height}}{\text{object height}}$ (no unit). This one is not on the equation list — a question that needs it gives it. Measure both on the same scale, with your eye directly above the ruler — the 2022 report's two warnings. To increase the magnification of a magnifying glass: use a fatter / more curved / shorter-focal-length lens, or move the object (further from the lens, but still inside F).

parts.question: An object is placed 5 cm from a converging lens of focal length 10 cm. Describe the image and name a device that uses the lens this way. (3 marks)

Image: the rays leaving the lens diverge, so the image is virtual, upright and magnified, on the same side of the lens as the object.
Device: a magnifying glass.

parts.title: Examples that come up
parts.html:

parts.title: A greenhouse
parts.question: Explain how a glass greenhouse stays warmer than the air outside. (3 marks)
steps: In: glass transmits the Sun's visible light and short-wavelength infrared, which are absorbed by the soil and plants, warming them.
Re-emission: the warm surfaces emit infrared of a longer wavelength (because they are much cooler than the Sun).
Trapped: glass absorbs (does not transmit) this longer-wavelength infrared, so the energy is kept inside and the temperature rises.

questions.text: Explain why the door of a microwave oven has a metal mesh with small holes. (2)
questions.model:
• Metal reflects microwaves: the holes are much smaller than the microwaves' wavelength (about 12 cm), so the mesh keeps them inside the oven.
  • Visible light has a wavelength far smaller than the holes, so it is transmitted and you can see the food.

questions.explain: The atmosphere transmits visible and radio but absorbs X-rays and gamma (and much of the ultraviolet and infrared, and some microwaves — the June 2022 Q6(c) scheme's examples). "Closer to the stars" is explicitly not accepted.

questions.text: A prism splits white light into a spectrum. Explain why. (3)

sections.blurb: Whether a substance absorbs, transmits, refracts or reflects an electromagnetic wave depends on the wavelength. Glass is transparent to visible light but absorbs most ultraviolet; the atmosphere lets radio and visible through but blocks X-rays. These explain colour, greenhouses, sunburn through windows and more.

sections.title: Radiate what you absorb: constant temperature and the Earth

parts.title: The four marks, in order
parts.html:
Every body absorbs radiation from its surroundings and emits radiation because of its own temperature. The rate at which it emits increases with its temperature. So:

  • If it absorbs power faster than it emits, its temperature rises — and as it warms it emits more, until…
  • …the rate of emission equals the rate of absorption: the temperature is then constant (thermal equilibrium).
  • If it emits faster than it absorbs, its temperature falls until the two rates are equal again.

The June 2023 scheme (Q8(b)(ii), 4 marks) and the June 2025 report (Q7(d), the dwarf planet Ceres) credit the same four points: (1) the body absorbs radiation; (2) it also emits radiation; (3) the rate of emission increases with temperature; (4) the temperature is constant when the rate of emission equals the rate of absorption. A fifth point, "mention of rate in (3) or (4)", is available, so any four of the five score — write rate (or power, accepted in 2025) in both (3) and (4) and the fourth mark is safe. "Heat" is accepted for radiation; "gives out / releases / loses" for emits; but "receives" was ignored in 2025 because it was in the stem — write absorbs. In June 2018 (Q8(c)(ii)) "at constant temperature the energy supplied = energy radiated" without rate scored 1 of the 2 marks: the rate is the physics.

The Earth absorbs radiation from the Sun (mostly visible) and emits infrared to space; its average temperature is set by that balance. Factors: clouds and ice reflect some incoming radiation back to space (less absorbed → cooler); greenhouse gases (carbon dioxide, methane, water vapour) absorb some of the outgoing infrared and re-emit it, some back towards the surface (less escapes → warmer); more greenhouse gas moves the balance to a higher temperature.

parts.title: The equilibrium answer
parts.question: A black metal plate is placed in sunlight. Its temperature rises for a while and then stays constant. Explain why. (4 marks)
steps: (1) The plate absorbs radiation from the Sun.
(2) It also emits radiation (infrared) because of its temperature.
(3) At first it absorbs faster than it emits, so it warms up; the rate of emission increases as its temperature rises.
(4) The temperature stops rising when the rate of emission equals the rate of absorption — constant temperature.

sections.title: Core practical: how a surface affects radiation
equations: \text{matt black: best emitter and best absorber}

parts.title: Emission: which surface radiates most?
parts.html:
Leslie cube: a hollow metal cube whose four faces are different — matt black, shiny black, white, shiny silver. Fill it with hot water and hold an infrared detector (or thermometer with a blackened bulb) the same distance from each face in turn; the detector reads highest for the matt black face and lowest for the shiny silver one.

Painted cans: the same with four identical cans painted different colours and finishes, each filled with the same volume of water at the same starting temperature; record the temperature every minute with a thermometer in each. The matt black can cools fastest (it emits most), the shiny silver can slowest.

Controls: same volume of water, same starting temperature, same can size, same distance from the detector, same time; a lid on each can so evaporation does not confuse the result. Why hot water? The hotter the surface, the more it radiates, so the differences are easier to measure.

parts.title: Absorption: which surface warms fastest?
parts.html:
Put the painted cans (with cold water, or metal plates with a thermometer attached) the same distance from a radiant heater or lamp and record the temperature every minute. The matt black can warms up fastest — it absorbs most of the radiation; the shiny silver can warms slowest — it reflects most.

Results to learn: matt black is the best emitter and the best absorber; shiny silver is the worst emitter and the worst absorber (the best reflector); white is a good reflector, poor absorber; matt surfaces beat shiny ones. A good absorber is always a good emitter.

The June 2023 scheme (Q8(b)(i), 2 marks) accepted any one full comparison: "black is a better absorber", "white is a better reflector", "black absorbs the radiation and white reflects it".

parts.title: Explaining the result
parts.question: Two identical cans of hot water, one painted matt black and one shiny silver, are left to cool. Explain why the matt black can cools faster. (2 marks)
steps: Emission: a matt black surface is a better emitter of infrared radiation than a shiny silver one (which is a poor emitter / good reflector).
So: the black can transfers energy to the surroundings at a greater rate, its thermal store empties faster, and its temperature falls faster.

sections.title: Where the waves come from: circuits, atoms and nuclei

parts.title: Producing and absorbing
parts.html:
Radio waves are produced when an alternating current flows in an aerial: the oscillating electrons radiate waves of the same frequency as the current. When a radio wave is absorbed by a receiving aerial it does the reverse: it induces an oscillating current (an alternating voltage) of the same frequency, which the receiver amplifies. That is the 2022 Q9(c) Level-3 point: "electron oscillation in circuits" is the source of radio waves.

Changes in atoms: when an electron in an atom drops to a lower energy level it emits a wave whose frequency depends on the energy difference — visible light, ultraviolet, or X-rays for the big jumps in heavy atoms. Absorbing a wave does the opposite: it can lift an electron to a higher level (or, with enough energy, remove it — ionisation). Gamma rays come from changes in the nucleus (Topic 6).

Fluorescence (June 2024 Q5(b), 4 marks): ultraviolet is absorbed by electrons → they move to a higher energy level (become excited) → they fall back to a lower level, emitting energy → as visible light (a different, lower frequency than the UV absorbed). Security marks and fluorescent lamps use this.

parts.title: Compare how X-rays and radio waves are produced
parts.question: Compare X-rays and radio waves: their position in the spectrum, one use of each, and how each is produced. (6 marks, levelled)
steps: Position: both are electromagnetic (transverse, same speed in a vacuum); X-rays have a much higher frequency and shorter wavelength than radio waves (the two ends of the spectrum), carry more energy and are ionising; radio waves are low frequency, long wavelength, low energy and not ionising.
Uses: X-rays — medical imaging of bones, airport security; radio — broadcasting and communications.

Production: X-rays — electrons in an atom absorb energy and move to a higher energy level, then return to a lower level and lose the energy as radiation; the energy drop is large, so the wave emitted has a high frequency (an X-ray). Radio — an alternating current (electrons flowing up and down the aerial, continually changing direction) generates radio waves around the aerial, whose frequency equals the frequency of the oscillation.

The 2022 indicative content had three strands — the comparison (frequency, wavelength, energy, ionising), the uses of each, and the production step by step — and a top answer covers all three. The stem already said "electrons go through energy changes" and "electrons in circuits", so repeating those words scored nothing ("no credit is given for" them); the production strand was the one "very few candidates knew" (2022 report).

sections.title: EM calculations the hard way

parts.title: Standard form without losing marks
parts.html:
Use the ×10ˣ key, never "× 10 ^": $3$ ×10ˣ $8$ ÷ $2.8$ ×10ˣ $(-)7$. Write the answer in standard form with the right number of significant figures ($1.07 \times 10^{15}$ Hz), not as a string of zeros.

Subtracting in standard form (June 2025 Q5(b)(iii) asked for the change in the speed of blue light entering glass: speed in glass $= f \times \lambda_{\text{glass}} = 6.4 \times 10^{14} \times 350 \times 10^{-9} = 2.2 \times 10^{8}$ m/s, then $3.0 \times 10^{8} - 2.2 \times 10^{8} = 0.8 \times 10^{8} = 8 \times 10^{7}$ m/s — the subtraction was an independent mark, and the report spoke of "keeping control of the standard form and mixed units"): write both numbers with the same power of ten first. $7.5 \times 10^{14} - 4.3 \times 10^{14} = 3.2 \times 10^{14}$. If the powers differ, convert one: $7.5 \times 10^{14} - 9.0 \times 10^{13} = 7.5 \times 10^{14} - 0.9 \times 10^{14} = 6.6 \times 10^{14}$.

Time for light to travel: $t = \dfrac{d}{v}$ with $v = 3 \times 10^{8}$ m/s and $d$ in metres (km × 1000). Sun to Earth, $1.5 \times 10^{11}$ m: $t = 500$ s, about 8 minutes.

Lens power: 20 cm is 0.20 m; $P = 1/0.20 = 5$ D. A diverging lens has a negative focal length and so a negative power. Finish the calculation — the 2022 report: candidates stopped at $1/f$ without working out $f$.

parts.title: The refraction practical in full
parts.question: Describe how a student could investigate how the angle of refraction of light entering a glass block depends on the angle of incidence. (6 marks)
steps: Step 1 — variables. I will change the angle of incidence and measure the angle of refraction, using the same glass block throughout.
Step 2 — relationship. I expect r to increase with i but to stay smaller than i, because light bends towards the normal as it slows in the glass.
Step 3 — change. Put the block on paper and draw round it; aim a narrow ray from the ray box at one face and change the angle of incidence by rotating the ray box, from about 10° to 70° in 10° steps.

Step 4 — measure. Mark the incident and emergent rays with crosses, remove the block, join the crosses and the entry–exit points; draw the normal at the entry point with a protractor and measure i and r from the normal with the protractor.
Step 5 — use the results. Plot a graph of angle of refraction against angle of incidence and describe its shape.
Step 6 — accuracy. Use a single narrow slit on the ray box and put the crosses far apart along each ray so the lines are accurate; work in a dim room.
Step 7 — repeat. Repeat each angle three times and calculate a mean angle of refraction.

facts.q: Law of reflection?
facts.a: Angle of incidence = angle of reflection, both measured from the normal.

facts.q: What is the normal?
facts.a: A line at 90° to the surface at the point where the ray hits. Draw it first; measure every angle from it.

facts.q: Specular vs diffuse reflection?
facts.a: Specular: smooth surface, parallel rays stay parallel, an image forms. Diffuse: rough surface, normals vary, rays scattered, no image. The law holds for both.

facts.q: Which way does light bend entering glass?
facts.a: Towards the normal — because it slows down.

facts.q: Which way does light bend leaving glass?
facts.a: Away from the normal — because it speeds up. The emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray.

facts.q: What causes refraction?
facts.a: A change in speed at the boundary. The part of the wavefront that changes speed first turns the wave.

facts.q: Refraction: what happens to speed, wavelength, frequency (light into glass)?
facts.a: Speed decreases, wavelength decreases, frequency unchanged.

facts.q: A ray along the normal?
facts.a: Does not change direction (angle of incidence 0°). It still slows down.

facts.q: Sound entering water?
facts.a: Speeds up (≈1500 m/s from 340 m/s) and bends away from the normal — the opposite of light.

facts.q: Define the critical angle.
facts.a: The angle of incidence (in the denser medium) at which the angle of refraction is 90° — the refracted ray runs along the surface.

facts.q: Two conditions for total internal reflection?
facts.a: Light going from a denser to a less dense material, and angle of incidence greater than the critical angle.

facts.q: Critical angle of glass, roughly?
facts.a: About 42°. Water about 49°.

facts.q: What happens at i = critical angle, and above it?
facts.a: At it: refracted ray along the surface ($r = 90$°). Above it: total internal reflection — all the light reflects inside.

facts.q: Why does a red object look red?
facts.a: It reflects red light and absorbs all the other colours.

facts.q: What does a blue filter do?
facts.a: Transmits blue light and absorbs the other colours.

facts.q: A red object in blue light looks…
facts.a: Black: there is no red to reflect, so it absorbs the blue.

facts.q: Converging lens: what does it do?
facts.a: Brings parallel rays together to a focus (principal focus F). Convex, fatter in the middle.

facts.q: Diverging lens: what does it do?
facts.a: Spreads parallel rays out as if from a focus on the near side. Concave, thinner in the middle. Negative focal length.

facts.q: Power of a lens equation and unit?
facts.a: $P = 1/f$, f in metres, P in dioptres (D). Converging positive, diverging negative.

facts.q: Power and shape?
facts.a: More curved (fatter, thicker in the middle) → shorter focal length → higher power.

facts.q: Three properties shared by all EM waves?
facts.a: Transverse; same speed in a vacuum (3 × 10⁸ m/s); transfer energy from source to observer.

facts.q: Speed of EM waves in a vacuum?
facts.a: 3 × 10⁸ m/s. Use it as v in $v = f\lambda$.

facts.q: Prefixes: GHz, MHz, nm?
EM spectrum in order of increasing frequency?
facts.a: Radio, microwaves, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma. (Raging Martians Invaded Venus Using X-ray Guns.)

facts.q: Which end has the longest wavelength? the highest frequency?
facts.a: Radio: longest wavelength, lowest frequency. Gamma: shortest wavelength, highest frequency.

facts.q: Visible light: colours in order of increasing frequency?
facts.a: Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet (red ≈ 700 nm, violet ≈ 400 nm).

facts.q: Why is the spectrum described as continuous?
facts.a: No gaps between the groups; the groups overlap at their edges.

facts.q: Uses of radio waves?
facts.a: Broadcasting, communications, satellite transmissions.

facts.q: Uses of microwaves?
facts.a: Cooking, communications (mobile phones), satellite transmissions.

facts.q: Uses of infrared?
facts.a: Cooking, thermal imaging, short-range communications, optical fibres, TV remote controls, security systems.

facts.q: Uses of ultraviolet?
facts.a: Security marking, fluorescent lamps, detecting forged bank notes, disinfecting water.

facts.q: Uses of X-rays?
facts.a: Observing the internal structure of objects, airport security scanners, medical X-rays.

facts.q: Uses of gamma rays?
facts.a: Sterilising food and medical equipment, detecting and treating cancer.

facts.q: How does danger vary across the spectrum?
facts.a: Potential danger increases with increasing frequency.

facts.q: Harm from microwaves? infrared?
facts.a: Microwaves: internal heating of body cells. Infrared: skin burns.

facts.q: Harm from ultraviolet? X-rays and gamma?
facts.a: UV: damage to surface cells and eyes → skin cancer, eye conditions. X and gamma: mutation or damage to cells → cancer.

facts.q: Does a cold object emit radiation?
facts.a: Yes — all bodies emit, mostly infrared at everyday temperatures.

facts.q: Hotter body: what changes about its radiation?
facts.a: Intensity increases; peak wavelength gets shorter (red → yellow → white hot).

facts.q: Four marks for "why is its temperature constant"?
facts.a: Absorbs radiation; also emits radiation; rate of emission rises with temperature; constant when rate of emission = rate of absorption. Say rate (or power) — it is a mark on its own.

facts.q: Body radiates more than it absorbs?
facts.a: Its temperature falls (until the rates balance). Less than it absorbs: temperature rises.

facts.q: How do greenhouse gases warm the Earth?
facts.a: They absorb some of the infrared the surface emits and re-emit it, some back down, so less escapes; the balance moves to a higher temperature.

facts.q: How do clouds and ice cool the Earth?
facts.a: They reflect incoming radiation back to space, so less is absorbed.

facts.q: Best emitter and absorber of radiation?
facts.a: Matt black. Worst: shiny silver (best reflector).

facts.q: Leslie cube: what is it?
facts.a: A metal cube with matt black, shiny black, white and shiny silver faces, filled with hot water; a detector at equal distance from each face compares emission.

facts.q: Controls in the cooling-cans experiment?
facts.a: Same volume of water, starting temperature, can size, distance; lids on; read every minute.

facts.q: How are radio waves produced?
facts.a: By an alternating current (oscillating electrons) in an aerial; when absorbed they induce an alternating current of the same frequency in a receiving aerial.

facts.q: Where do visible, UV and X-rays come from in an atom?
facts.a: Electrons dropping from a higher to a lower energy level. Gamma rays come from the nucleus.

facts.q: Fluorescence in four steps?
facts.a: UV absorbed by electrons → raised to a higher level → fall back → emit visible light (lower frequency).

facts.q: Time for light from the Sun?
facts.a: $t = d/v = 1.5 \times 10^{11} \div 3 \times 10^8 = 500$ s, about 8 minutes.

facts.q: Subtracting in standard form?
facts.a: Write both with the same power of ten first, then subtract the front numbers.

facts.q: Refraction practical: the six steps?
facts.a: Draw round the block; narrow ray in; crosses on incident and emergent rays; remove block and join; normal + protractor for i and r; repeat angles and plot r against i.

facts.q: Why a semicircular block for the critical angle?
facts.a: A ray aimed at the centre of the flat face enters along a normal to the curved face, so it does not bend on entry.

facts.q: Critical angle from an i–r graph?
facts.a: Extend the curve to $r = 90$° and read off i.

facts.q: Converging lens, object beyond 2F?
facts.a: Real, inverted, smaller, between F and 2F on the far side (camera).

facts.q: Converging lens, object between F and 2F?
facts.a: Real, inverted, magnified, beyond 2F on the far side (projector).

facts.q: Converging lens, object inside F?
facts.a: Virtual, upright, magnified, same side as the object (magnifying glass).

facts.q: Diverging lens image?
facts.a: Always virtual, upright and smaller, on the object's side.

facts.q: Real vs virtual image?
facts.a: Real: rays actually meet, can be projected on a screen, inverted. Virtual: rays only appear to come from it, cannot be projected, upright.

facts.q: Magnification equation?
facts.a: image height ÷ object height (same scale, no unit).

facts.q: Why no sunburn through glass?
facts.a: Glass transmits visible light but absorbs most ultraviolet.

facts.q: Why are X-ray telescopes in space?
facts.a: The atmosphere absorbs X-rays (and gamma and UVC); it transmits visible and radio.

facts.q: State what is meant by: normal.
facts.a: A line at 90° to the surface at the point where the ray meets it; angles are measured from it.

facts.q: State what is meant by: angle of incidence.
facts.a: The angle between the incident ray and the normal.

facts.q: State what is meant by: angle of refraction.
facts.a: The angle between the refracted ray and the normal (inside the second material).

facts.q: State what is meant by: reflection.
facts.a: Light bouncing off a surface; angle of incidence = angle of reflection.

facts.q: State what is meant by: refraction.
facts.a: The change of direction of a wave when it crosses a boundary, caused by a change of speed.

facts.q: State what is meant by: specular reflection.
facts.a: Reflection from a smooth surface: parallel rays stay parallel, forming an image.

facts.q: State what is meant by: diffuse reflection.
facts.a: Reflection from a rough surface: rays are scattered in many directions because the normal varies.

facts.q: State what is meant by: critical angle.
facts.a: The angle of incidence (in the denser medium) at which the angle of refraction is 90°.

facts.q: State what is meant by: total internal reflection.
facts.a: All the light is reflected back inside the denser medium, when the angle of incidence is greater than the critical angle.

facts.q: State what is meant by: converging lens.
facts.a: A lens (convex, fatter in the middle) that brings parallel rays together to a focus.

facts.q: State what is meant by: diverging lens.
facts.a: A lens (concave, thinner in the middle) that spreads parallel rays apart, as if from a focus on the near side.

facts.q: State what is meant by: focal length.
facts.a: The distance from the centre of the lens to the principal focus.

facts.q: State what is meant by: power of a lens.
facts.a: 1 ÷ focal length (in metres), in dioptres; higher power = more curved = shorter focal length.

facts.q: State what is meant by: real image.
facts.a: An image formed where rays actually meet; it can be projected onto a screen; usually inverted.

facts.q: State what is meant by: virtual image.
facts.a: An image formed where rays appear to come from; it cannot be projected onto a screen; upright.

facts.q: State what is meant by: transverse wave.
facts.a: A wave whose oscillations are at right angles (perpendicular) to the direction the wave travels (the direction of energy transfer) — all EM waves.

facts.q: State what is meant by: frequency.
facts.a: The number of waves per second, in hertz (Hz).

facts.q: State what is meant by: wavelength.
facts.a: The distance from one point on a wave to the same point on the next wave (e.g. crest to crest), in metres.

facts.q: State what is meant by: ionising radiation.
facts.a: Radiation with enough energy to remove electrons from atoms (ionise them): UV, X-rays, gamma.

types.name: EM waves: v = f × λ with c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s
types.method: All electromagnetic waves travel at 3 × 10⁸ m/s in a vacuum (and almost that in air), so for an EM wave the speed is already known: v = 3 × 10⁸ m/s. Use v = f × λ to find the frequency (f = v ÷ λ) or the wavelength (λ = v ÷ f). Convert first: kHz × 10³, MHz × 10⁶, GHz × 10⁹; nm × 10⁻⁹, mm × 10⁻³, cm × 10⁻². Use the ×10ˣ key and give large or small answers in standard form.
commonErrors: Leaving GHz, MHz or nm unconverted — the 2022 report: "learn the multiples of units to be able to use correct powers of 10"
Multiplying v by f when the question wants a wavelength instead of dividing
Writing 300 000 000 with the wrong number of zeros instead of 3 × 10⁸
Using the speed of sound (340 m/s) for a radio wave or light

v = f × λ → λ = v ÷ f

types.name: Power of a lens: P = 1 ÷ f
equations: f in metres, P in dioptres (D)
types.method: The power of a lens is 1 divided by its focal length, with the focal length in metres. The unit is the dioptre, D. A converging lens has a positive power; a diverging lens has a negative focal length and so a negative power. A shorter focal length (a fatter, more curved lens) means a higher power. To find the focal length from the power, f = 1 ÷ P — and finish the calculation: the 2022 report says candidates stopped at 1/f.
commonErrors: Leaving the focal length in centimetres (20 cm gives P = 0.05 D instead of 5 D)
Stopping at 1/f = 0.25 instead of finishing f = 4 m — or giving 1/P instead of P
Forgetting the minus sign for a diverging lens
Writing the unit as m or W instead of D (dioptres)

worked.question: A converging lens has a focal length of 20 cm. Calculate its power.
steps: Known: f = 20 cm = 0.20 m. Unknown: P.
P = 1 / f
P = 5 D
